briefs.headline: Finances for raising a child
briefs.deck: Data and inflation models suggest raising a child to age 25 costs a middle-class semi-urban or urban household ₹75 lakh -₹2 crore and an upper-middle-class family ₹2-4 crore, depending on lifestyle and city
briefs.bodyText:
Over two decades, India’s parenting economics have shifted dramatically. Raising a child was once a low-cost endeavour; today, in a semi-urban and urban India, navigating a child’s life from the delivery room to a postgraduate convocation demands meticulous, data-backed wealth management.
Data and inflation models suggest raising a child to age 25 costs a middle-class semi-urban or urban household ₹75 lakh -₹2 crore and an upper-middle-class family ₹2-4 crore, depending on lifestyle and city.
The figures are a baseline for proactive planning not a cause for panic. Understanding the data and harnessing long-term compounding lets parents secure a child’s future without compromising on their own financial independence.
Expenses in three phases
Phase 1: Foundation Years (age 0-5). Maternity care, delivery and post-natal healthcare at private hospitals usually cost ₹1-₹5 lakh. Vaccinations, paediatric visits, diapers and nutrition add up while preschools and daycare in cities cost ₹1-2 lakh a year. Likely phase cost: ₹10-20 lakh.
Phase 2: Schooling Marathon (age 6-17). Sustained cash flow gets tested here. Annual fee at a private or international board school cost ₹1.5-4 lakh; extracurriculars, ed-tech subscriptions and lifestyle costs: yearly outflow reaches ₹3.5-6.5 lakh. Estimated phase cost: ₹40-80 lakh.
Phase 3: Higher Education Climax (age 18-25). The most capital-intensive hurdle. While inflation averages 5-6%, education inflation runs at 10-12% a year. A professional degree in commerce, engineering, medicine or arts can cost ₹25 lakh-₹1.5 crore, rising to ₹3 crore with a master’s and PhD. If a shortfall remains, education loan interest stays fully deductible under Section 129 (formerly section 80E) for up to eight years. Estimated phase cost: ₹25 lakh to ₹3 crore.
The math seems daunting, but the solution is straightforward: start early, choose vehicles that systematically outpace education inflation.
Harness early equity
Time is your greatest asset. Starting a systematic investment plan (SIP) in diversified equity funds the month your child is born gives an 18-year compounding runway. Equity is the only asset class that beats 10-12% education inflation over the long term. An SIP of ₹20,000-30,000 a month, stepped up 10% annually, can build a pre-tax corpus of ₹2.88-₹4.32 crore at an assumed 12% CAGR and ₹3.89-5.83 crore at 15% over 18 years.
Tax-efficient govt. schemes.
For the debt portion, the public provident fund (PPF) offers tax-free compounding and for a daughter, the Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY) offers tax-free returns. Both qualify for the ₹1.5 lakh deduction under section 123 (formerly section 80C). NPS Vatsalya, a minor’s NPS account that converts into a regular NPS account at 18, carries an additional ₹50,000 deduction under section 124 (formerly 80CCD(1B)), over and above the section 123 limit.
Risk-management wall
Wealth creation is futile without protection. Primary breadwinners should secure term life insurance worth 15-20 times annual income so a child’s education stays funded even after an untimely demise. A comprehensive family health insurance policy is equally non-negotiable, protecting the corpus from being liquidated during medical emergencies. Raising a child to 25 is a multi-decade commitment comparable with funding a small enterprise though the returns are immeasurable. Acknowledging the data, factoring in education inflation and automating investments from day one turns financial anxiety into financial empowerment, building a launchpad for your child’s future.
(The writer is founder - Rupee With Rushabh Investment Services)

stories.headline: Ronaldo's Portugal return possible? Coach Jesus clears the air
stories.deck: Portugal coach Jorge Jesus has left the door open for Cristiano Ronaldo to return after the 41-year-old left the squad last week. Jesus said the decision is Ronaldo’s, while federation president Pedro Proenca backed the captain and called the episode a misunderstanding. Ronaldo remains Portugal’s record scorer and most-capped player, with 146 goals in 234 appearances.
stories.bodyText:
Portugal coach Jorge Jesus has kept the door open for Cristiano Ronaldo to return to the national team after the 41-year-old captain left the squad last week. Ronaldo departed after being left on the bench against Norway and told he would not start against Denmark, later saying he would explain his decision "in due course".
"If he wants to, he'll return to the national team. We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who's going to decide," Jesus said, as quoted by news agency Reuters, after Portugal beat Norway 2-1.
"He's the one who should decide how he wants to end his time with the national team. In my first call-up, I said, 'I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you'. And now I'm saying the same thing."
Portugal won without Ronaldo against Denmark before beating Norway to reach the Nations League quarter-finals. Ronaldo remains the country's record scorer and most-capped player, with 146 goals in 234 appearances.
Portugal still counting on Ronaldo
Portuguese Football Federation president Pedro Proenca also said Ronaldo remains part of the team's plans and described his departure as a misunderstanding that should be handled internally.
"He is in the national team on sporting merit, and that must be unquestionable," Proenca told RTP. "We have to pay tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo."
Jesus, who previously coached Ronaldo at Al-Nassr, expects the forward could return during the next international break if he chooses. Portugal will host Denmark on November 14 before travelling to Wales three days later.

stories.headline: England pacer with 500-plus wickets ends career, citing mental health
stories.deck: English fast bowler Craig Miles has retired from professional cricket at 32 to prioritise his mental health. The Gloucestershire pacer, who last played in June, ends a 15-year career with more than 500 wickets. Miles said mounting pressure, self-doubt and high expectations made continuing difficult. He reflected proudly on his career, while Gloucestershire praised his courage and backed his…
stories.bodyText:
English fast bowler Craig Miles has announced his retirement from professional cricket at the age of 32, saying he needs to step away to protect his mental health.
Miles, who last played in June during the Vitality Blast, finishes a 15-year career with more than 500 wickets across formats.
In an open letter published by Gloucestershire, Miles explained that his recent struggles with cricket had become too difficult to manage.
"It’s with sadness, but also with huge pride, that I can announce my retirement from professional cricket. Although this has by no means been an easy decision, given the struggles I've experienced with the game in recent times, I've made this call in order to prioritise my mental well-being," he wrote.
"My recent time away from the game has given me the opportunity to reflect and understand myself better, as well as my relationship with cricket. The challenges I've faced recently are ones I've experienced at other points in my career, although never with the same intensity as this time. The high expectations I place on myself and the standards I've always tried to reach, have often been the catalyst for these periods.
"At times, they have compromised how I've felt about my abilities and performances. The questioning and self-doubt that follow only serve to reinforce an unhelpful narrative. When you add in the volatility and uncertainty that cricket naturally brings, it becomes an unforgiving and ultimately unsustainable way to approach the game."
Looking back on his career
Miles said he no longer felt capable of maintaining the standards he expected from himself, despite having enjoyed many successful periods in the sport.
"Unfortunately, I now feel I no longer have the capacity to continue in a way that allows me to train, play and perform to a standard I can accept from myself. Of course, there have also been so many periods when I’ve loved the game, played with freedom and truly expressed the player I am.
“A first-class debut at 16, more than 200 games, over 500 wickets, a One Day Cup and a Championship win - it’s been a pretty good go. I can appreciate those accomplishments more than ever now and, perhaps for the first time, give myself the self-validation I deserve.”
Gloucestershire director of cricket Jon Lewis called Miles' decision brave and said the club would fully support him as he moves away from professional cricket.

stories.headline: Ireland soccer players again wear black armbands and refuse handshakes with Israel team
stories.deck: Ireland players have again worn black armbands and bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem before the teams’ second Nations League soccer match
stories.bodyText:
Ireland players again wore black armbands and bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem before the teams’ second Nations League soccer match on Sunday (October 4, 2026).
The Israeli players also wore black armbands in memory of the people killed in the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher stepped in as captain for Dara O’Shea – who was excused to be with his wife for the birth of their child – and he pointedly avoided shaking hands with Israel captain Dor Peretz, despite completing the usual pre-match formality with the referee and one of his assistants.
Kelleher repeated O’Shea’s actions before the first match in Debrecen, Hungary last week, when O'Shea declined to shake Israel captain Manor Solomon's hand. Ireland went on to win that game 3-0 through three first-half goals.
Solomon was dropped to the bench for Sunday's (October 4, 2026) match in Backa Topola, Serbia. Israel forward Sayed Abu Farchi was back in the squad after serving a suspension for getting sent off following his goal celebration during Israel’s 3-1 defeat to Austria on Sept. 25.
Finn Azaz, whose mother has Israeli heritage, was among the Irish substitutes after playing from the start against Austria on Thursday.
Sunday's (October 4, 2026) game was initially supposed to be played in Dublin, but the Football Association of Ireland moved the game to a neutral venue for “operational reasons” in June following widespread calls for a boycott in protest of Israel’s actions in Gaza. The FAI said the game would be played with no fans present.
It followed the FAI’s own motion the previous November calling on UEFA to ban Israel from club and international competitions.
All the Irish players had been under pressure from home, where affinity with Palestinians is strong, to boycott the second match against Israel, though they faced the greatest pressure before the first game. Ultimately only reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazuno decided to skip both of the contentious games, saying in a statement that it was his “personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong.”
Protesters threw tennis balls with Palestinian flags onto the field during Ireland’s 2-2 draw with Austria on Thursday (October 1, 2026), when a man with a Palestinian flag also later tried running onto the field.
On Saturday (October 3, 2026), an Israeli journalist stated during the pre-match press conference that the Irish players had called the Israeli players “monkeys” during last week’s game, leading to an immediate rebuke from Irish communications officer Kieran Crowley, who said it was “a lie” and ended the press conference.
The players only decided to go ahead with the fixtures after a dramatic day in Debrecen before the first match, when both press conference and training were delayed for hours while they deliberated. They reportedly voted 14-8 in favor of continuing after Bazunu’s withdrawal that morning.

stories.headline: The afterglow of the Asiad gold
stories.deck: For Shreyas, this was a much-needed victory. This campaign, away from probing eyes, would have facilitated his reintegration to progress further. The fact that he had most of his first-choice personnel around would have aided the process of refamiliarisation and put him in a good head-space
stories.bodyText:
To be installed the overwhelming favourite ahead of any major sporting extravaganza is a double-edged sword. The moniker is suggestive of a formidable individual (or team) clearly more skilled, more temperamentally adjusted, and the most likely to go all the way, but it also comes with a rider. You are marked; the rest will be doubly determined to hunt you down and add a coveted scalp to their kitty.
Long before a single ball was bowled at the Asian Games, the Indian men’s cricket team was fancied to come up trumps. The women too, of course, considering that they had just blazed to the Asia Cup in Dubai, sweeping everyone in front of them. Harmanpreet Kaur’s intrepid bunch kept its tryst with gold in commanding fashion, brooking no opposition and flexing its not inconsiderable muscle with aplomb. Immediately thereafter, the spotlight turned to Shreyas Iyer and his lads, up against four other continental Test-playing nations who chose to put out experimental rather than full-strength outfits.
One of the talking points in the lead-up to the Asiad was why India’s selectors had chosen to go with the tried and the tested. People harked back to the previous event in Hangzhou three years back, when Ruturaj Gaikwad led a second-string team to the gold medal after the final against Afghanistan was washed out, and wondered why a similar squad wasn’t pieced together. For more than one reason, it is apparent.
The previous Asian Games overlapped with the 50-over World Cup hosted by India, thereby comprehensively ruling out the presence in China of the main squad. There is no gainsaying what personnel the selectors would have picked in the absence of the said overlap; that’s delving into the realms of the hypothetical, which serves little purpose.
This time around too, India were involved in a three-match One-Day International series against West Indies at home; the first of the ODIs was played on September 27, a day before Shreyas’ boys began their title defence in the quarterfinal against Afghanistan. While there are several players who are certainties in both white-ball formats internationally, India weren’t too weakened by the absence from the 50-over set-up of Shreyas, the ODI vice-captain, and Ishan Kishan. Sure, they missed bowling spearheads Jasprit Bumrah and Axar Patel – Shubman Gill’s unit conceded more than 1000 runs to the Caribbeans in the three fixtures – but what is the weight of an ODI series with little immediate import compared to an Asian Games gold medal?
Cricket authorities have worked tirelessly in ensuring the inclusion of the sport in multi-discipline events like the Asian Games and the Olympic Games. The International Cricket Council’s avowed goal is to take the discipline to as many countries as possible. Having identified the 20-over format as the vehicle to drive that ambition, it has handed over memberships to a host of nations – the official T20I team rankings includes a staggering 102 countries – and conferred international status on matches involving even, say, Lesotho and Costa Rica, ranked 89th and joint-94th respectively.
Perfect sense
It therefore makes perfect sense to honour their presence in these big bashes by sending out the strongest team possible under the circumstances. Perhaps Shreyas might not say so publicly, but one is pretty certain that he would cherish an Asian Games gold medal more than being on the right side of a 2-1 scoreline against West Indies in a largely meaningless ODI series which, even with the World Cup a year away, was largely bereft of context. Batathons on flat tracks that took away the joy of a contest might have appealed to the spectators but it did little to edify the sport. But then, we digress.
Weight of favouritism
Shreyas and stand-in head coach V.V.S. Laxman were aware of the weight of favouritism imposed on the side. They also had the belief and the confidence that, never mind the relative strengths of their opponents, they would be unstoppable if they played at even 90% of their potential. Even at full strength, which Afghanistan were last month when they quixotically hosted India at Delhi’s Arun Jaitley Stadium, the rest of the field would have been hard pressed to stretch India. Given that Shreyas had all the big guns at his disposal, from Abhishek Sharma and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi to Sanju Samson and Kishan, and Bumrah and Axar, India had to play extraordinarily poorly and their opponents, whoever they might have been, had to play out of their skins to orchestrate an upset.
Banana skin
As their one-off T20I against Japan showcased last month, an abridged T20 game can be a banana skin. On a pitch that served as a horrible advertisement for a 5-overs-a-side affair, India huffed and puffed to a two-run victory. More than any other format, the 20-over slugfest narrows the gap between teams, and when that is reduced by 75%, the chances of a more level playing field increase exponentially.
Most pitches at the Asian Games weren’t up to scratch, favouring the bowling sides to a massive degree – how the Indian and West Indian 50-over exponents would have loved that – even though the final was played on a pretty good surface that produced more 400 runs. India’s overwhelming superiority was never more evident than in the semifinal against Sri Lanka when Kishan’s unbeaten 80 was nearly twice as much as what the entire opposition managed. India played with flair and imagination, and without the burden of expectations and fear. A lot of credit for that should go to Laxman, as good a man-manager as any the country has been blessed with but temporarily – one hopes – lost to the coaching spectrum because of personal reasons.
Laxman has now shepherded India to successive Asian Games gold medals, even though he might not individually have anything to show for it. Were he the sort, he would clamber on to the tallest rooftop and tom-tom about his contributions. But he didn’t do that when he was winning matches and shaping miracles for the country, so he is not going to embark on that journey now. In India, some people are more equal than others and that will never change, which is why Laxman’s contributions will inevitably fly under the radar though as a batter, few have influenced the outcomes of Test matches more than the stylist from Hyderabad.
One of the prime tenets of Laxman’s coaching philosophy is constancy and stability. Among the others is communication. During his playing career, Laxman suffered on both counts, so he is in a far better position to appreciate the significance of role clarity, of being made to feel wanted, and of being kept in the loop about developments so that no one is operating in a vacuum. Many of the players who travelled with him to Zimbabwe in July, immediately after the misadventures in Ireland and England, and to the Asian Games, have spoken in private of the positive influence of the 51-year-old and how his openness, approachability and his sense of balance and fairness have impacted them. Laxman is a firm believer in processes, but also in not rigidly sticking to them or making decisions on the fly, on a whim and a fancy. While no coach can ever be accused of winning or losing matches, it is undeniable that the environment they fashion within the changing room plays a massive part in how the wards approach the game. On that count, Laxman has few equals.
For Shreyas, this was a much-needed victory. Brought back to the T20I fold after two and a half years and installed as the captain with India deciding to move on from Suryakumar Yadav – World Cup-winning skipper but short on runs – he must have felt the heat after surrendering 0-2 to Ireland and 0-4 to England in his first two assignments. The clean sweep against Afghanistan last month must have lifted his morale, but this campaign, away from probing eyes, would have facilitated his reintegration to progress further. The fact that he had most of his first-choice personnel around would have aided the process of refamiliarisation and put him in a good headspace, imperative because he is the designated ODI vice-captain and will be expected to play a big part with the bat at No. 4 in the lead-up to and during the World Cup.
Shreyas knows he has a great bunch to work with. He will have taken particular joy in the sustained good form of Kishan, for whom 2026 has heralded a breathtaking second coming, and the continued development as a batter, an individual and leader of Tilak Varma, his T20I deputy. Like he had in the Asia Cup final in Dubai in September last year when he steered India past Pakistan in a tense run-chase, the left-hander from Hyderabad upped his game against the old foe in the title clash on Saturday, his unbeaten 51, off just 22 deliveries, pushing the total past 200 and out of reach of a spirited Pakistan well served by the exciting Hasan Nawaz.
Tilak was batting at No. 6, somewhat below his normal and preferred position because India stacked up their batting even if it meant they were a bowler light. He walked in with just 41 deliveries left in the innings and made a spectacular impact, showing how far he has come in international cricket. Just 23 months back, in South Africa towards the end of 2024, he sought to occupy the No. 3 position that Suryakumar had made his own. When the skipper acquiesced, Tilak expressed his thanks with two hundreds in three nights, in Centurion and adjacent Johannesburg respectively. Now, he doesn’t need the No. 3 position, which puts him in a position to play more balls than anyone else but the two openers, to unfurl his repertoire and shape the destination of 20-over games, which is exactly the kind of graph one would expect of a 23-year-old who is desperate to be a permanent for the country across formats.
Already, the Asian Games adventure is a thing of the past, what with the five-match T20I series against West Indies due to begin in Lucknow on Tuesday. A vast chunk of those who travelled to Japan will line up in the administrative and legislative capital of Uttar Pradesh, as a new challenge beckons. West Indies have shown in the ODIs that they are no pushovers and India will have their work cut out. And while they know that it doesn’t guarantee victory, Shreyas and his boys will still bask in the afterglow of an Asian Games gold medal. Whyever not?

briefs.headline: England crush Croatia 7-0 as Spain stay perfect with Czech victory
briefs.deck: England ⁠are second in League A, Group Three with six points from three matches, behind Spain on nine
briefs.bodyText:
Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka scored twice apiece as England demolished Luka Modric's Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka on Saturday, but Spain stayed three points clear at the top of their Nations League group with a 3-1 victory over the Czech Republic.
Jude Bellingham scored once and provided three assists for England, with Anthony Gordon and substitute Morgan Rogers also on target in a performance captain Kane described as "unbelievable".
England are second in League A, Group Three with six points from three matches, behind Spain on nine. Croatia have three points and the Czechs remain pointless.
"Unbelievable from start to finish," Kane told ITV. "We spoke a lot about having a 90-minute game from start to finish, being completely dominant with the ball and without the ball. That was it right there."
Kane took his international tally to 89 goals in 124 appearances, moving within one cap of Peter Shilton's England record.
Asked about potentially drawing level with Shilton against the Czech Republic on Tuesday, Kane said: "Would be nice. That is why he (manager Thomas Tuchel) takes me off, to save me for the next one!"
England went ahead after little more than seven minutes when Josko Gvardiol lost possession and Bellingham released Kane, who slipped between two defenders and fired home.
Bellingham doubled the lead in the 21st minute after Gordon turned Saka's cross back across goal. Gordon added the third in the 39th, meeting Jarell Quansah's cross with a first-time finish.
Mateo Kovacic squandered a close-range chance before Bellingham crossed for an unmarked Saka to score a minute before halftime.
Elliot Anderson supplied Kane's second goal with a low cross in the 53rd minute, before Josip Stanisic's misplaced pass across his own box gifted Saka another goal in the 68th.
Bellingham released Rogers to complete the rout three minutes from time.
"They couldn't live with our pace, with our runs," Kane said.
SPAIN KEEP WINNING
World and European champions Spain maintained their perfect start in Oviedo despite coach Luis de la Fuente making nine changes to the side that beat Croatia 4-1 on Tuesday.
Lamine Yamal opened the scoring in the sixth minute, curling a stunning left-footed shot into the top corner from the edge of the box.
After Spain squandered several opportunities, captain Rodri doubled their advantage by converting a rebound inside the area, his first international goal in more than two years.
Jiri Slama gave the visitors hope in the 69th minute, finishing a swift counter-attack with an angled shot just inside David Raya's right post.
Their chances of an equaliser faded when Ladislav Krejci received a second booking in the 85th minute for holding back an opponent to stop a counter-attack.
Mikel Merino then sealed Spain's victory, finishing first time from inside the box following another quick break.
In League B, Scotland won 2-0 at North Macedonia through goals from Kieron Bowie and John McGinn before Scott McKenna was sent off in the 83rd minute.
Switzerland came from behind to beat Slovenia 2-1 in Luzern, with an Erik Janza own goal and Dan Ndoye's strike overturning Zan Vipotnik's opener. The Swiss lead Group One on nine points, with Scotland and Slovenia level on four.

briefs.headline: Max Verstappen washes away frustrations with win at Bahrain Grand Prix
briefs.deck: The ​four-time Formula 1 drivers’ champion earned his first win of 2026 ‌and the 72nd of his decorated career
briefs.bodyText:
Max Verstappen flushed away at least some of his seasonlong frustrations Sunday (October 4, 2026) by winning the rain-delayed Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
The four-time Formula 1 drivers’ champion earned his first win of 2026 and the 72nd of his decorated career when he waited out a 1-hour, 33-minute delay at the outset and then held off current drivers’ standings leader Kimi Antonelli at the finish.
George Russell, who was still alive with an outside chance at catching Mercedes AMG Motorsport teammate Antonelli for the drivers’ title, saw those hopes take a blow due to an engine failure with five laps remaining.
After a season in which Verstappen struggled to adapt to changes to F1 cars, the rest of the field was able to feel his pain for a day. Those new cars struggled to operate in the wet conditions, leading to an initial 40-minute delay at the start and then another 53-minute delay when software issues plagued some cars, including Verstappen’s.
“It was very hectic with a lot of different things in the start,” Verstappen said. “No power, so you have to wait for the power to kick in. But then we made the right call with the intermediates, and after that, step by step, we moved our way forward.”
When the race finally started, Verstappen dropped from his position on the pole into third place before passing Antonelli on Lap 13, and went on to win from there, finishing 2.3 seconds ahead of the standings leader. Lewis Hamilton was third after rallying from 18th place.
“It’s a really nice one, after the year that we’ve had and the progression that we’ve made,” Verstappen said. “I’m incredibly proud of everyone, and it’s just super nice to win here.”
Charles Leclerc finished fourth, while Isack Hadjar was fifth.
Hadjar was one of the first drivers to be impacted by the early conditions when he lost control on Turn 2 of the formation lap and was forced into the gravel. Verstappen and Hamilton then reported engine issues.
A red flag was issued as drivers took a more cautious approach than usual in the early going.
Russell’s issues arrived after Alexander Albon saw his car stall. With the safety car on the track on Lap 43, Russell came to a stop just before heading into Turn 1.
Verstappen maintained his lead on the restart and went on to the victory.

briefs.bodyText:
The Tamil Nadu u-23 team just cannot stop clinching titles. Having achieved a double in the previous season, it added a trophy to its cabinet after defeating Rest of India u-23 in a match that mirrored the Irani Cup.

They are good enough to win the tournaments again,” said Andre, proudly sporting a victor’s medal around his neck.
The u-23 unit will begin its Col. C.K. Nayudu Trophy defence in a home game against Saurashtra in Dindigul later this month. With Andre becoming a mainstay in the senior red-ball set-up, the age-group side will be led by all-rounder S. Mohamed Ali. “These guys are too good to be honest. I have been playing with them since my u-12 days. They know what they need to do... these aren’t guys who need to be told what is expected of them,” Andre added.
For RoI opener Angkrish Raghuvanshi, it was about getting back in the groove.
The Mumbai lad had been out of action for three months with a finger injury, but he is now finding his feet again. The double century against TN u-23 was a massive confidence booster. “I am playing [competitive cricket] after a long time and my knock gave me clarity. The middle of the pitch is my happy place,” said Raghuvanshi.
“I tried to bat as long as I could. It was a satisfying experience because every batter dreams of hitting big hundreds. It was a good day for me, but it would have been better had we won the match,” he added.

briefs.headline: IND vs WI ODIs review: Men in Blue’s bowling remains a red mark even as batters extend purple patch
briefs.deck: Apart from Kuldeep in the first match, none of the bowlers looked like they could keep the batters honest or provide timely breakthroughs
briefs.bodyText:
With just about a year to go for the 2027 ODI World Cup, India’s preparation for the quadrennial event got off on the right note as it posted a 2-1 series win over the West Indies.
There were, however, some warning signs that the team will want to address soon.
The big positive was the batting. The top-order set up the series victory, led by skipper Shubman Gill, who scored two centuries, including a double hundred.
More importantly, Rohit Sharma (225 runs) and Virat Kohli (168) were on song. Since this is the only format they play, it is imperative the senior duo maximises every opportunity.
K.L. Rahul got only one chance and proved why he is so vital to the team, scoring an unbeaten 129, even if it went in vain.
However, bowling remains a concern. Granted, the pitches at all three venues had very little for the bowlers. Still, the attack is hardly settled.
Apart from Kuldeep Yadav in the first match, none of the others looked like they could keep the batters honest or provide timely breakthroughs.
The other fast bowlers not being able to take up responsibility showed how the Men in Blue are over-reliant on Jasprit Bumrah, who was away on Asian Games duty.
The management handed out debuts to Auqib Nabi and Anshul Kamboj, both of whom proved expensive while Mohammed Siraj’s recent struggle continued in the only match he played. Captain Gill admitted as much, saying he would have wanted to see more out of his speedsters.
“Bowling in the PowerPlay and in the death has been hurting us. If you don’t get off to a good start in the PowerPlay, it’s not easy to take wickets in the middle overs as we have seen,” said Gill.
“It’s not easy to create chances with only four fielders outside. The intensity of the game, and how it goes, becomes completely different if you don’t keep taking wickets in either the PowerPlay or the middle overs,” he added.
Going forward, the think-tank needs to quickly identify the right combination for the World Cup and give them enough games to get into a groove, something Gill stressed he wants to do from the next series.

briefs.headline: ‘Thanks for the gift’: Pant’s 29th birthday made special as RoI reclaim Irani Cup
briefs.deck: Rishabh Pant's birthday happened to coincide with a remarkable comeback as the Rest of India triumphed over Jammu and Kashmir in the Irani Cup. Despite falling behind initially, the team rallied to secure a 167-run victory. Although Pant missed the action due to illness, he joined in the post-match festivities. Mukesh Kumar's exceptional bowling and young talent Ravichandran Smaran's innings were…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Rishabh Pant
 could not have asked for a better 29th birthday present. On a day when he missed the action because of fever, the Rest of India captain watched his teammates complete a stunning comeback against Jammu and Kashmir to reclaim the Irani Cup before joining the celebrations with the trophy and cake.
Rest of India, after conceding a 41-run first-innings lead to the Ranji Trophy champions, bowled out J&K for just 111 in their chase of 279 on Sunday to seal a commanding 167-run victory at the Sher-i-Kashmir Stadium.
Pant, who made 10 and eight in the match, did not take the field on the fourth day, with 
Sarfaraz Khan
 taking over as on-field captain. But his leadership was evident in the way Rest of India responded after falling behind early.
‘We just kept on fighting’
Addressing his teammates after the victory, Pant said the squad had been driven by the desire to restore pride after going without the Irani Cup for two years.
“Guys, great effort. In the last 5-7 days, we were discussing that let's play for the pride and let's play for our monogram. No matter what happens, especially in the first innings, they did a good batting effort and they took the first innings lead,” Pant said in a video posted by BCCI Domestic.
“But, in the dressing room, whatever they do, we need to focus on ourselves. Obviously, most of the time, the game went in their favour.”
The captain praised his teammates for refusing to let the match slip away.
“One thing for sure, our Rest of India team, we didn't let it go. We just kept on fighting with every ounce of intensity we had. One day, one over, one ball at a time and, everyone contributed in their own way,” he said.
“From last two years, we were not winning. But, we made sure that when we leave this ground, we put our name on the trophy as winners.”
‘Thanks for the gift’
The celebrations became even more special with Pant’s birthday falling on the day of the triumph.
In a video shared by BCCI Domestic, his teammates and coaches gathered around the wicketkeeper-batter and sang ‘Happy Birthday’ in chorus. Ground staff members also offered their blessings and wishes before Pant cut the cake and posed with the trophy alongside his teammates.
“Thanks for the gift,” a smiling Pant said as the dressing-room celebrations continued.
The captain also explained how a tactical adjustment in bowling helped turn the contest around.
“Mostly the plan was to bowl fuller in the first innings. That was the conversation we had with the bowlers that we were like, we would back up the length,” Pant said at the post-match presentation.
“That was something we wanted to correct in the second innings because we knew our bowlers were really good, but the problem was the first innings we bowled too much back of the length, and we corrected that and bowled fuller and fuller in the second innings.”
Mukesh Kumar led the demolition with 6-33 as J&K collapsed after lunch.
Pant also reserved special praise for young batter Ravichandran Smaran, who scored 68 in the first innings before producing a match-winning 135 in the second.
“Today all the pieces fell in place, but at the same time, you know, like you mentioned, Smaran, the way he played in both innings, I think it was outstanding innings, especially we were under pressure, especially in the second innings the way he played, it was outstanding,” Pant said.

briefs.headline: Asian Games: PM Modi congratulates Team India, hails ‘passion and sporting spirit’
briefs.deck: Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised the inspiring performances of Indian athletes at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, where India clinched a remarkable total of 85 medals, including 21 golds, finishing fourth overall. The Games were highlighted by record-breaking efforts, particularly in athletics, showcasing the talent of emerging athletes. Modi called for enhanced focus on grassroots sports…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday congratulated the Indian contingent for its performance at the Aichi-Nagoya 
Asian Games
, praising the athletes for representing the country with “determination, passion and remarkable sporting spirit” as India concluded its campaign with 85 medals.
India finished fourth on the medal table with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals, ending the Games with its second-highest medal haul in Asian Games history. The tally was 21 medals fewer than the record 106 won at the Hangzhou edition in 2023.
As the Games drew to a close in Nagoya on Sunday, Modi took to X to applaud the entire contingent and the medal winners while also expressing hope that the performances would help strengthen Indian sport at the grassroots level.
‘Immense joy to the nation’
In his post, the Prime Minister praised the athletes for their effort and sporting spirit throughout the continental showpiece.
“As the Asian Games 2026 draw to a close, my compliments to every member of the Indian contingent for representing our nation with determination, passion and remarkable sporting spirit. Congratulations to all our medal winners, whose performances have brought immense joy to the nation. 
May these Games inspire even greater achievements in the years ahead. May they contribute to strengthening sports at the grassroots too,” Modi wrote.
The Prime Minister’s message came after more than two weeks of competition involving athletes from 45 countries. The Aichi-Nagoya Games witnessed a string of record-breaking performances, including 54 world records.
The Games formally concluded with a spectacular closing ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium in Nagoya on Sunday.
Historic golds and landmark performances
India’s campaign was marked by several historic performances and successful title defences across disciplines.
Both Indian cricket squads retained their Asian Games titles, while the men’s and women’s kabaddi sides also won gold. The men’s hockey side successfully defended its title with a 5-1 victory over Malaysia, while the women’s team ended a 44-year wait for an Asian Games gold by defeating China 1-0 in the final.
There were also several breakthrough individual performances.
Pranavi Urs became the first Indian woman to win an individual Asian Games golf gold, while 17-year-old archer Kumkum Mohod created history by becoming the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold at the continental showpiece.
Mohod was also part of India’s historic women’s recurve team gold that ended South Korea’s seven-edition winning streak in the event. Wrestler Sujeet Kalkal, meanwhile, produced one of the most dramatic comebacks of the Games to win the men’s 65kg freestyle gold.
Boxer Lovlina Borgohain also joined an elite group of Indian women by becoming only the second after Mary Kom to win an Asian Games boxing gold.
Looking beyond Aichi-Nagoya
Athletics emerged as India’s biggest medal contributor with 24 medals, while shooting accounted for 15. Archery was the most successful sport in terms of gold medals, producing five top finishes.
The campaign also provided a series of important milestones ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, with several young athletes making their mark on the continental stage.
Earlier, 
Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha named Mohod and Kalkal the inaugural recipients of the Jaspal Rana Award and Raja Randhir Singh Award respectively
 for the best female and male Indian sportspersons of the Games.
With the Aichi-Nagoya campaign now complete, Modi’s message placed the emphasis not only on India’s medal tally but also on the broader legacy of the Games — inspiring another generation of athletes and strengthening the sporting ecosystem from the grassroots upwards.

briefs.headline: Lionel Messi's long road from 'outsider' to Argentina’s undisputed leader
briefs.deck: Messi moved to Barcelona as a teenager. While Spain tried to convince him to play for them, Argentina had limited knowledge of the youngster from Rosario.
briefs.bodyText:
When 
Lionel Messi
 makes his final appearance for Argentina against Benin on Tuesday at Buenos Aires’ Monumental stadium, it will mark the end of an international career that has lasted more than two decades.
It will also bring the curtain down on a relationship that took time to develop. Argentina’s football authorities once struggled even to identify the teenage Messi, who was developing his career far from home. Over the years, he went from being viewed with suspicion to becoming the leader of the national team and one of the most important figures in Argentine football.
"He went through so many moments that they're really very different eras. At first he suffered enormously with the national team. He truly endured it," Argentine journalist and author Sergio Levinsky, who wrote "Messi and Everything Else", told news agency Reuters.
Messi moved to Barcelona as a teenager. While Spain tried to convince him to play for them, Argentina had limited knowledge of the youngster from Rosario.
At the 2003 Under-17 World Cup in Finland, Spain beat Argentina 3-2 after extra time in the semi-finals. 
According to Levinsky, Cesc Fabregas, who scored twice in the match and was Messi’s teammate at Barcelona’s La Masia academy, told Argentine delegates after the game: "You lost to us because we've got your best player at Barcelona and he's a genius."
Argentina youth coach Hugo Tocalli recalled a similar conversation. Speaking at the Ole Summit last month, he said Spain’s head chef told him Argentina needed "a kid who plays in Barcelona" to win the tournament.
The Argentine Football Association (AFA) then had to find the teenager who was already making an impression in Spain.
AFA employee Omar Souto tracked down the Messi family through a Rosario telephone directory, but when he made contact, he asked for "Leonardo".
"His name isn't Leonardo, it's Lionel," Souto was told, according to the documentary "Messi: The Forgotten Tape".
Even Messi’s name caused confusion in the paperwork. Levinsky said the AFA sent Barcelona a fax asking about a player called "Mecci", spelling the surname with a double "c" because officials believed he might be Italian.
A love under construction
Messi eventually played two under-20 friendlies for Argentina in 2004, making his first appearances in the blue and white shirt. But doubts about him remained.
At the 2005 Under-20 World Cup in the Netherlands, Messi started on the bench as Argentina lost their opening game.
"There was strong resistance to calling up a kid who didn't play in the country," Levinsky said, as quoted by Reuters. "He had to fight against those early suspicions, against being considered a foreigner because he lived in Spain."
Messi was later criticised for not producing the same level of football for Argentina that he did for Barcelona. Some fans even labelled him "pecho frio", suggesting he lacked heart or fire.
A World Cup qualifier against Colombia in 2011 became an important moment in changing that perception. Messi helped Argentina recover from a goal down in difficult conditions.
"He was exhausted, even vomiting, and he ended up winning," Levinsky said. "It was the first time fans saw him differently."
The relationship grew stronger after Messi briefly retired from international football following Argentina’s penalty shootout defeat by Chile in the 2016 Copa America final. Instead of blaming him, Argentine fans publicly urged him to return.
"People realised he was not responsible for the defeats. He was the one getting them to finals," Levinsky added.
Under Lionel Scaloni, Messi became the clear leader of a new generation of Argentine players. He guided the team to two Copa America titles and the 2022 FIFA World Cup.
As Messi became a more vocal captain, comparisons with Diego Maradona became inevitable. But Levinsky believes the debate over who was Argentina’s greater player misses the bigger picture.
"It is Messi and Maradona," he added. "They were both geniuses in different eras."
"Messi was like suddenly finding out you have an 18-year-old son," Levinsky said. "You have to start loving him without having known he existed. It was a love under construction."
